mainTopic: Why מגילת תענית listed the third of תשרי, which holidays need reinforcement days, and whether מגילת תענית was cancelled after the חורבן
overview: The גמרא asks why מגילת תענית had to list the third of תשרי as a day without fasting. In the time of the בית המקדש, the day גדליה בן אחיקם was killed was already a happy day. רב answers that the listing was needed to forbid fasting on the day before, the second of תשרי. The גמרא asks whether that day is already covered because it comes after ראש חודש, or because it comes before the day of גדליה. The answer to both is no. A ברייתא teaches that Torah-level days do not need 'reinforcement' days around them, and רב אשי adds that דברי קבלה count like Torah law. Then רב טובי בר מתנה challenges the view that מגילת תענית was cancelled after the חורבן. He points out that a new festive day, the 28th of אדר, was added to it after a Roman decree was overturned. The גמרא shows this happened after the חורבן, because יהודה בן שמוע, who led the protest, was a student of רבי מאיר. It begins proving this from a משנה about glass vessels, and that proof continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Why list the third of תשרי if it is already גדליה's day?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why מגילת תענית needed to forbid fasting on the third of תשרי, since it is the day גדליה בן אחיקם was killed, which was already a festive day in the time of the בית המקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: But you could get this rule from the fact that it is the day that גדליה בן אחיקם was killed!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the need for the listing in מגילת תענית. It says the third of תשרי is already a non-fasting day for another reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: While the בית המקדש stood, the fast days mourning the חורבן were turned into days of joy, including the fast of גדליה on the third of תשרי. If the day was already festive, adding it to מגילת תענית seems to add nothing. The גמרא wants to know what the listing accomplishes.

keyTerms.meaning: But derive it from (a different, simpler reason)
The governor of יהודה after the חורבן, whose murder is mourned on the third of תשרי
A scroll listing days on which fasting is forbidden because of happy events

phrases.english: But derive it from the fact that it is the day
phrases.notes: In the time of the בית המקדש, the fast days for the חורבן became happy days (זכריה 8:19). That is why this question works.

phrases.english: on which Gedaliah son of Ahikam was killed!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתִיפּוֹק לֵיהּ דְּהָוֵה לֵיהּ יוֹם שֶׁנֶּהֱרַג בּוֹ גְּדַלְיָה בֶּן אֲחִיקָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the earlier statement on the daf that מגילת תענית lists the third of תשרי.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for מגילת תענית to list the third of תשרי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The day was already festive in Temple times as the day of גדליה, so the listing seems unnecessary.

steps.title: רב: The listing was needed to forbid the day before
steps.stepSummary: רב answers that the listing was needed to forbid fasting on the day before the third, which is the second of תשרי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: It was only needed in order to forbid fasting on the day before it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב explains what the listing in מגילת תענית adds. Days in מגילת תענית also forbid fasting on the day before them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The third of תשרי itself did not need the listing. However, listing a day in מגילת תענית also forbids fasting on the days around it. So the real point of the listing is the second of תשרי.

phrases.english: Rav said:
It was only needed
to forbid the day before it.
phrases.notes: He means forbidding fasting on the second of תשרי.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: לֹא נִצְרְכָה אֶלָּא לֶאֱסוֹר אֶת שֶׁלְּפָנָיו
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shifts the purpose of the listing to a different day
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The listing was meant to make the third of תשרי itself a non-fasting day.
steps.terutzMaskana: The listing's real job is to forbid fasting on the second of תשרי.

steps.title: The day before is already the day after ראש חודש
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks that the second of תשרי is already forbidden because it is the day after ראש חודש.
steps.simpleTranslation: The day before should also be covered already, since it is the day after ראש חודש!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's answer. It says the second of תשרי already has a reason not to fast, because it comes right after ראש חודש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If special days forbid fasting on the days next to them, then ראש חודש on the first of תשרי should forbid fasting on the second. Then רב's explanation would also leave the listing with nothing to add.

keyTerms.meaning: The first day of the month; the first of תשרי is ראש חודש

phrases.english: The day before it, too,
derive it from the fact that it is
the day after the New Moon!
phrases.notes: The second of תשרי comes right after the first, which is ראש חודש.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁלְּפָנָיו נָמֵי, תִּיפּוֹק לֵיהּ דְּהָוֵה לֵיהּ יוֹם שֶׁלְּאַחַר רֹאשׁ חֹדֶשׁ
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's claim that the listing was needed for the day before
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The second of תשרי is already next to ראש חודש, so it should already be forbidden for fasting.

steps.title: Torah holidays do not need reinforcement
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that ראש חודש is a Torah-level day, and Torah-level days do not need extra protection on the days around them.
steps.simpleTranslation: ראש חודש is from the Torah, and something from the Torah does not need reinforcement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. Being next to ראש חודש does not forbid fasting, because ראש חודש is from the Torah.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule about forbidding the days around a holiday is a 'reinforcement' (חיזוק). Rabbinic days need it so people take them seriously. Torah days are respected on their own, so the second of תשרי is not forbidden because of ראש חודש.

phrases.english: The New Moon is from the Torah,
and what is from the Torah does not need reinforcement.

steps.triggerLanguage: רֹאשׁ חֹדֶשׁ דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא, וּדְאוֹרָיְיתָא לָא בָּעֵי חִיזּוּק
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes between Torah-level and rabbinic-level days
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every special day forbids fasting on the day after it, including ראש חודש.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only rabbinic days get extra 'reinforcement' days. Torah days like ראש חודש do not, so the second of תשרי still needs the listing.
steps.confusionAlert: It may seem backwards that the Torah days get less protection. The idea is that Torah days are strong enough on their own, while rabbinic days need extra protection.

steps.title: A ברייתא: מגילת תענית days need reinforcement, שבת and יום טוב do not
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא proves the rule: the days of מגילת תענית forbid fasting before and after them, but שבת and יום טוב do not, because Torah laws need no reinforcement and rabbinic laws do.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: These days written in מגילת תענית are forbidden for fasting, both the day before them and the day after them. שבתות and ימים טובים are themselves forbidden, but the days before and after them are allowed. What is the difference? These are Torah law, and Torah law needs no reinforcement. Those are rabbinic law, and rabbinic law needs reinforcement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to support its answer from step 4. The ברייתא spells out the difference between Torah holidays and rabbinic holidays.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא sets the two types of days side by side. מגילת תענית days are rabbinic, so fasting is also forbidden on the days around them. שבת and יום טוב are Torah days, so fasting is allowed on the days around them. This is the exact principle the גמרא used for ראש חודש.
steps.whatToRemember: Rabbinic holidays (like the days of מגילת תענית) need 'reinforcement' days before and after them. Torah holidays (like שבת, יום טוב and ראש חודש) do not.

phrases.english: As it was taught: These days
that are written in Megillat Ta'anit are forbidden,
both the day before them and the day after them.
Shabbatot and Festivals: they themselves are forbidden,
but the days before them and after them are permitted.
What is the difference between this and that?
These are Torah law,
and Torah laws do not need reinforcement.
Those are rabbinic law,
phrases.notes: Now "those" means the days of מגילת תענית.

phrases.english: and rabbinic laws need reinforcement.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא: הַיָּמִים הָאֵלֶּה הַכְּתוּבִין בִּמְגִילַּת תַּעֲנִית אֲסוּרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to back up the principle stated in step 4.
steps.raayaObject: The principle that Torah-level days do not need reinforcement
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא contrasting the days of מגילת תענית with שבת and יום טוב
steps.whyThisMatters: This ברייתא gives the basic rule for the whole discussion, and the next challenge and answer are built on it.

steps.title: The second of תשרי is the day before גדליה's day
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks that the second of תשרי is already forbidden because it is the day before the festive day of גדליה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But you could get this from the fact that it is the day before the day that גדליה בן אחיקם was killed!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new challenge to רב. Even if ראש חודש does not count, the second of תשרי comes right before the festive day of גדליה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Temple times the third of תשרי was a happy day. If happy days forbid fasting on the day before, the second of תשרי is already covered. Then the listing in מגילת תענית would again add nothing.

phrases.english: But derive it from the fact that it is
the day before the day
on which Gedaliah son of Ahikam was killed!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתִיפּוֹק לֵיהּ דְּהָוֵה לֵיהּ יוֹם שֶׁלִּפְנֵי יוֹם שֶׁנֶּהֱרַג בּוֹ גְּדַלְיָה בֶּן אֲחִיקָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second attack on רב's answer, now that the ראש חודש attack was answered.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's claim that the listing was needed for the day before
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The second of תשרי is next to the festive day of גדליה, so it should already be forbidden for fasting.

steps.title: רב אשי: דברי קבלה are like Torah law
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that the day of גדליה comes from דברי קבלה, which are treated like Torah law, so it does not need reinforcement days.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: The day of גדליה בן אחיקם is from דברי קבלה, and דברי קבלה are like Torah law.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers the last challenge. The day of גדליה does not forbid fasting on the day before it, because it is treated like a Torah-level day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fast of גדליה, and its becoming a happy day, come from the נביאים (דברי קבלה). For this rule, דברי קבלה count like Torah law, which does not need reinforcement. So only the listing in מגילת תענית forbids fasting on the second of תשרי, and רב's answer stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Teachings from the נביאים and כתובים
Are similar to, are treated like

steps.whatToRemember: The listing of the third of תשרי in מגילת תענית is needed to forbid fasting on the second of תשרי. Neither ראש חודש (Torah law) nor the day of גדליה (דברי קבלה, treated like Torah law) adds reinforcement days.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:

phrases.aramaic: גְּדַלְיָה בֶּן אֲחִיקָם דִּבְרֵי קַבָּלָה הוּא,
phrases.english: Gedaliah son of Ahikam is from the words of tradition,
phrases.notes: "Words of tradition" means the books of the נביאים and כתובים, where this fast is mentioned.

phrases.english: and the words of tradition are like Torah law.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: גְּדַלְיָה בֶּן אֲחִיקָם דִּבְרֵי קַבָּלָה הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 6 using the principle from the ברייתא in step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Puts דברי קבלה in the same group as Torah law
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The day of גדליה is not a Torah law, so it would need reinforcement like a rabbinic day.
steps.terutzMaskana: דברי קבלה are treated like Torah law and do not need reinforcement. So the second of תשרי is forbidden only because of מגילת תענית.
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets up an important category: laws from the נביאים and כתובים can be treated like Torah law.

steps.title: רב טובי quotes the 28th of אדר from מגילת תענית
steps.stepSummary: רב טובי בר מתנה begins an objection by quoting the entry in מגילת תענית for the 28th of אדר, a day of good news after a harsh Roman decree.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב טובי בר מתנה objected: On the 28th of the month, good news came to the Jews that they would not have to turn away from the Torah. The wicked kingdom had made a decree that Jews must not learn Torah, must not circumcise their sons, and must break שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a challenge. רב טובי quotes a day from מגילת תענית and starts to tell its background story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point of quoting this day will become clear soon: it is a day that was added to מגילת תענית late in history. For now we only learn what the decree was: no Torah, no מילה, and forced חילול שבת.

keyTerms.meaning: an early list of happy days on which fasting is forbidden

phrases.english: Rav Tovi bar Mattana raised an objection:
On the twenty-eighth of it
phrases.notes: "Of it" means the month of אדר, which this part of מגילת תענית is listing.

phrases.english: good tidings came to the Jews
that they should not turn away from the Torah.
For the wicked kingdom issued a decree
that they should not occupy themselves with Torah,
and that they should not circumcise their sons,
and that they should desecrate Shabbat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a challenge against the view that מגילת תענית was nullified.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that מגילת תענית was nullified after the חורבן.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Setup only: the source being quoted will show a day added to the list after the חורבן.

steps.title: The protest that cancelled the decree
steps.stepSummary: יהודה בן שמוע and his friends follow a Roman noblewoman's advice, protest at night, and get the decrees cancelled. That day becomes a festive day.
steps.simpleTranslation: What did יהודה בן שמוע and his friends do? They asked advice from a noblewoman whom all the important men of Rome visited. She told them to go and cry out at night. They did, saying: Heavens! Aren't we your brothers, children of one father and one mother? Why are we different from every other nation, that you make such harsh decrees against us? The decrees were cancelled, and that day was made a festive day.
steps.whatsHappening: This continues the story behind the 28th of אדר. It tells how the decree was cancelled and the day became a festive day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key detail for the argument is the name יהודה בן שמוע, because it tells us when this happened. The ending, that they made the day a יום טוב, shows the day was added to מגילת תענית.

phrases.aramaic: מָה עָשָׂה יְהוּדָה בֶּן שַׁמּוּעַ וַחֲבֵירָיו?
phrases.english: What did Yehuda ben Shammua and his colleagues do?
They went and took advice
from a certain noblewoman
whom all the important men of Rome would regularly visit.
She said to them:
Come and cry out at night.
They went and cried out at night,
they said: O Heavens!
Are we not your brothers,
and are we not children of one father,
and are we not children of one mother?
How are we different from every nation and tongue
that you issue harsh decrees against us?
And they annulled them.
And that day they made into a festive day.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה עָשָׂה יְהוּדָה בֶּן שַׁמּוּעַ וַחֲבֵירָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the quoted story behind the 28th of אדר.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The day the decrees were cancelled was made a יום טוב in מגילת תענית.

steps.title: Would they cancel old days and add new ones?
steps.stepSummary: רב טובי's punch line: if מגילת תענית was nullified, it makes no sense that new days were still being added to it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you think מגילת תענית was nullified, would they cancel the first days and then add new ones?!
steps.whatsHappening: Here the objection lands. If the old days were cancelled, why would the חכמים add a new day like the 28th of אדר?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Adding a new festive day shows that מגילת תענית was still in force when it was added. So if this day was added after the חורבן, the list cannot have been nullified at the חורבן.

phrases.english: And if it enters your mind
that Megillat Ta'anit was nullified,
the first ones they annulled,
and later ones they add?!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ בָּטְלָה מְגִילַּת תַּעֲנִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the challenge out of the quoted source.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that מגילת תענית was nullified.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Days were still being added to the list, so it must still have been in force.

steps.title: This could not have happened while the Temple stood
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects a possible answer, that this day was also added while the בית המקדש stood. יהודה בן שמוע was a student of רבי מאיר, who lived after the חורבן.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say that this too happened while the בית המקדש was standing: but יהודה בן שמוע was a student of רבי מאיר, and רבי מאיר lived after that!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא blocks a way out of the question. Someone might say this day was added before the חורבן, but the timeline shows it was added afterward.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'it was added before the חורבן' would save the view that the list was nullified at the חורבן. But יהודה בן שמוע was a student of רבי מאיר, and רבי מאיר lived after the חורבן, so יהודה בן שמוע did too. That means the day was added after the חורבן, and the question stands.

keyTerms.meaning: while the בית המקדש was standing

phrases.english: And if you say

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא נָמֵי בִּזְמַן שֶׁבֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ קַיָּים
phrases.english: here too it was when the Temple was standing
but Yehuda ben Shammua
was a student of Rabbi Meir,
and Rabbi Meir lived after that!
phrases.notes: "After that" means after the בית המקדש was destroyed.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא הָכָא נָמֵי בִּזְמַן שֶׁבֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ קַיָּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Strengthens the קשיא by heading off a possible answer.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The suggested answer that the 28th of אדר was added before the חורבן.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The timeline: יהודה בן שמוע was a student of רבי מאיר, who lived after the חורבן.

steps.title: Proof that יהודה בן שמוע was רבי מאיר's student
steps.stepSummary: A משנה about glass vessels patched with lead shows יהודה בן שמוע quoting a ruling in the name of רבי מאיר.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned in a משנה: About glass vessels that got holes and someone dripped lead into them, רבן שמעון בן גמליאל said: יהודה בן שמוע rules them impure in the name of רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a משנה to prove that יהודה בן שמוע was רבי מאיר's student. The quote continues past this point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, יהודה בן שמוע passes on a ruling 'in the name of רבי מאיר'. That shows he learned from רבי מאיר, which backs up the timeline used in the previous step.

phrases.english: As we learned in a mishna:
Glass vessels that got holes
and one dripped lead into them,
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said:
Yehuda ben Shammua rules them impure
in the name of Rabbi Meir,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the claim made in the previous step that יהודה בן שמוע was רבי מאיר's student.
steps.raayaObject: That יהודה בן שמוע was a student of רבי מאיר.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about glass vessels patched with lead.
